questions.question_html: When 1 g of compound $(X)$ is subjected to Kjeldahl's method for estimation of nitrogen, 15 mL 1 M $H_{2}SO_{4}$ was neutralized by ammonia evolved. The percentage of nitrogen in compound $(X)$ is :
questions.explanation_text: In Kjeldahl’s method, the ammonia ( $NH_{3}$ ) evolved neutralizes the acid taken. So, $\text{equivalents of}H_{2}SO_{4}=\text{equivalents of ammonia}$ Given: $15\text{mL}$ of $1\text{M}H_{2}SO_{4}$ is neutralized. $H_{2}SO_{4}$ is a dibasic acid, so $1$ mole of $H_{2}SO_{4}$ gives $2$ equivalents. Therefore, equivalents of $H_{2}SO_{4}$ used are: $\frac{15 \times 1 \times 2}{1000}$ Ammonia is monobasic (one $NH_{3}$ neutralizes one equivalent of acid), so: $\frac{15 \times 1 \times 2}{1000}=\text{moles of ammonia} \times 1$ So, moles of ammonia $=$ moles of nitrogen ( $N$ ), because each mole of $NH_{3}$ contains $1$ mole of $N$ . Now, mass of nitrogen: $\text{Weight of nitrogen}=\frac{15 \times 1 \times 2}{1000} \times 14=0.42$ Percentage of nitrogen in $1\text{g}$ compound: $%\text{weight of ’}N\text{’}=\frac{0.42}{1} \times 100=42%$
questions.explanation_html:
In Kjeldahl’s method, the ammonia ( $NH_{3}$ ) evolved neutralizes the acid taken. So,

$\text{equivalents of}H_{2}SO_{4}=\text{equivalents of ammonia}$

Given: $15\text{mL}$ of $1\text{M}H_{2}SO_{4}$ is neutralized.

$H_{2}SO_{4}$ is a dibasic acid, so $1$ mole of $H_{2}SO_{4}$ gives $2$ equivalents. Therefore, equivalents of $H_{2}SO_{4}$ used are:

$\frac{15 \times 1 \times 2}{1000}$

Ammonia is monobasic (one $NH_{3}$ neutralizes one equivalent of acid), so:

$\frac{15 \times 1 \times 2}{1000}=\text{moles of ammonia} \times 1$

So, moles of ammonia $=$ moles of nitrogen ( $N$ ), because each mole of $NH_{3}$ contains $1$ mole of $N$ .

Now, mass of nitrogen:

$\text{Weight of nitrogen}=\frac{15 \times 1 \times 2}{1000} \times 14=0.42$

Percentage of nitrogen in $1\text{g}$ compound:

$%\text{weight of ’}N\text{’}=\frac{0.42}{1} \times 100=42%$

questions.question_text: In Dumas method for estimation of nitrogen, 0.50 g of an organic compound gave 70 mL of nitrogen collected at 300 K and 715 mm pressure. The percentage of nitrogen in the organic compound is $____$ $%$ . (Aqueous tension at 300 K is 15 mm ).
questions.question_html:
In Dumas method for estimation of nitrogen, 0.50 g of an organic compound gave 70 mL of nitrogen collected at 300 K and 715 mm pressure. The percentage of nitrogen in the organic compound is $____$ $%$ .

(Aqueous tension at 300 K is 15 mm ).
questions.explanation_text: In Dumas method, the nitrogen gas collected over water contains water vapour also. So first we find the pressure of dry nitrogen gas by subtracting aqueous tension. $\begin{aligned} & P_{N_{2}}=(715-15)mm=\frac{700}{760}atm \\ & V_{N_{2}}=70ml=\frac{70}{1000}l \end{aligned}$ Now use the ideal gas equation $n=\frac{PV}{RT}$ to calculate moles of nitrogen gas. $\begin{aligned} & n_{N_{2}}=\frac{PV}{RT}=\frac{(\frac{700}{760}) \times (\frac{70}{1000})}{0.0821 \times 300} \end{aligned}$ Mass of nitrogen obtained is moles $\times$ molar mass of $N_{2}$ (which is $28gmol^{-1}$ ). $\begin{aligned} & W_{N_{2}}=\frac{700}{760} \times \frac{\frac{70}{1000}}{0.0821 \times 300} \times 28 \end{aligned}$ Finally, percentage of nitrogen in the compound is : $\begin{aligned} & %N=\frac{W_{N_{2}}}{0.5} \times 100=\frac{700}{760} \times \frac{\frac{70/1000}{0.0821 \times 300} \times 28}{0.5} \times 100 \\ & =14.65% \approx 15 \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
In Dumas method, the nitrogen gas collected over water contains water vapour also. So first we find the pressure of dry nitrogen gas by subtracting aqueous tension.

$\begin{aligned} & P_{N_{2}}=(715-15)mm=\frac{700}{760}atm \\ & V_{N_{2}}=70ml=\frac{70}{1000}l \end{aligned}$

Now use the ideal gas equation $n=\frac{PV}{RT}$ to calculate moles of nitrogen gas.

$\begin{aligned} & n_{N_{2}}=\frac{PV}{RT}=\frac{(\frac{700}{760}) \times (\frac{70}{1000})}{0.0821 \times 300} \end{aligned}$

Mass of nitrogen obtained is moles $\times$ molar mass of $N_{2}$ (which is $28gmol^{-1}$ ).

$\begin{aligned} & W_{N_{2}}=\frac{700}{760} \times \frac{\frac{70}{1000}}{0.0821 \times 300} \times 28 \end{aligned}$

Finally, percentage of nitrogen in the compound is :

$\begin{aligned} & %N=\frac{W_{N_{2}}}{0.5} \times 100=\frac{700}{760} \times \frac{\frac{70/1000}{0.0821 \times 300} \times 28}{0.5} \times 100 \\ & =14.65% \approx 15 \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: Analysis of Statement (I) : 1,2,3-Trihydroxypropane is commonly known as glycerol. In the soap industry, it is found mixed with water in a solution called 'spent lye'. Glycerol has a very high boiling point (around $563\text{K}$ or $290^{\circ}\text{C}$ ) and it has a tendency to decompose at or below its normal boiling point. Because of this risk of decomposition under continuous heating at normal atmospheric pressure, simple distillation cannot be used. Instead, the standard technique prescribed for its separation is distillation under reduced pressure (also known as vacuum distillation). By reducing the pressure on the surface of the liquid, the mixture can boil at a much lower temperature, which prevents the glycerol from decomposing. Therefore, Statement (I) is false. Analysis of Statement (II) : An azeotrope, or an azeotropic mixture, is defined as a binary mixture having the exact same composition in both the liquid phase and the vapour phase. Because the vapour has the same proportions of components as the unboiled liquid, the mixture boils at a constant temperature, acting almost like a single pure liquid. Fractional distillation relies on the principle that the vapour phase will be richer in the more volatile component. Since an azeotropic mixture does not show any change in composition upon vaporization, the components cannot be separated into their pure fractions by fractional distillation. Therefore, Statement (II) is completely true. Conclusion : Since Statement (I) is false because distillation under reduced pressure must be used, and Statement (II) is fundamentally true according to the properties of azeotropes, the correct logical match is Option D. Correct Answer : Option D : Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.explanation_html:
Analysis of Statement (I) :

1,2,3-Trihydroxypropane is commonly known as glycerol. In the soap industry, it is found mixed with water in a solution called 'spent lye'. Glycerol has a very high boiling point (around $563\text{K}$ or $290^{\circ}\text{C}$ ) and it has a tendency to decompose at or below its normal boiling point. Because of this risk of decomposition under continuous heating at normal atmospheric pressure, simple distillation cannot be used.

Instead, the standard technique prescribed for its separation is distillation under reduced pressure (also known as vacuum distillation). By reducing the pressure on the surface of the liquid, the mixture can boil at a much lower temperature, which prevents the glycerol from decomposing. Therefore, Statement (I) is false.

Analysis of Statement (II) :

An azeotrope, or an azeotropic mixture, is defined as a binary mixture having the exact same composition in both the liquid phase and the vapour phase. Because the vapour has the same proportions of components as the unboiled liquid, the mixture boils at a constant temperature, acting almost like a single pure liquid.

Fractional distillation relies on the principle that the vapour phase will be richer in the more volatile component. Since an azeotropic mixture does not show any change in composition upon vaporization, the components cannot be separated into their pure fractions by fractional distillation. Therefore, Statement (II) is completely true.

questions.explanation_text: Diethyl amine + Ethyl amine (A) : Ethyl amine ( $CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{2}$ ) is a primary ( $1^{\circ}$ ) aliphatic amine, whereas diethyl amine ( $(CH_{3}CH_{2})_{2}NH$ ) is a secondary ( $2^{\circ}$ ) aliphatic amine. Primary amines answer the Carbylamine test (or isocyanide test). When warmed with chloroform ( $CHCl_{3}$ ) and alcoholic potassium hydroxide ( $KOH$ ), primary amines produce a foul-smelling substance called isocyanide. Secondary and tertiary amines do not show this reaction. Therefore, A matches with II. Acetaldehyde + Acetone (B) : Acetaldehyde ( $CH_{3}CHO$ ) is an aldehyde, while acetone ( $CH_{3}COCH_{3}$ ) is a ketone. Aldehydes can be distinguished from ketones using Tollens' test . When treated with Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal silver nitrate), aldehydes get oxidized to carboxylate ions, and the silver ions are reduced to form a brilliant silver mirror on the inner walls of the test tube. Ketones do not respond to this test. Therefore, B matches with IV. Ethanol + Phenol (C) : Phenol ( $C_{6}H_{5}OH$ ) has an $OH$ group attached directly to an aromatic ring, which gives a characteristic violet or purple colouration when treated with Neutral $FeCl_{3}$ solution due to the formation of a coordination complex. Ethanol ( $CH_{3}CH_{2}OH$ ), being an aliphatic alcohol, does not react with neutral $FeCl_{3}$ . Therefore, C matches with III. Benzoic acid + Cinnamic acid (D) : Cinnamic acid ( $C_{6}H_{5}-CH=CH-COOH$ ) is an unsaturated acid as it contains a carbon-carbon double bond in its side chain. It responds to the test for unsaturation and will rapidly decolorize the reddish-brown colour of Bromine water . Benzoic acid ( $C_{6}H_{5}COOH$ ) does not have any aliphatic unsaturation and thus will not decolorize bromine water. Therefore, D matches with I. questions.explanation_text: Statement I is true. In Lassaigne’s test, the organic compound is fused with sodium metal. During this fusion, elements present in the covalent organic compound are converted into ionic sodium salts. For example, $\text{C, N}\overset{\text{Na}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}NaCN$ $\text{S}\overset{\text{Na}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}Na_{2}S$ $\text{X}\overset{\text{Na}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}NaX$ So, covalent organic molecules are changed into ionic compounds. Hence, Statement I is true. Statement II is false. If an organic compound contains both nitrogen and sulphur, then during sodium fusion it generally forms sodium thiocyanate: $Na+C+N+S \rightarrow NaSCN$ Sodium thiocyanate gives a blood-red colour with ferric ions due to formation of ferric thiocyanate complex, not Prussian blue. Prussian blue colour is obtained in the test for nitrogen when sodium cyanide is formed: $NaCN+FeSO_{4} \rightarrow Na_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]$ On acidification, it gives Prussian blue. But for a compound having both N and S together, the characteristic test is blood-red colour due to thiocyanate, not Prussian blue. So, the correct answer is: $\text{Option D: Statement I is true but Statement II is false}$
questions.explanation_html:
Statement I is true.

In Lassaigne’s test, the organic compound is fused with sodium metal. During this fusion, elements present in the covalent organic compound are converted into ionic sodium salts.

For example,

$\text{C, N}\overset{\text{Na}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}NaCN$

$\text{S}\overset{\text{Na}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}Na_{2}S$

$\text{X}\overset{\text{Na}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}NaX$

So, covalent organic molecules are changed into ionic compounds. Hence, Statement I is true.

Statement II is false.

If an organic compound contains both nitrogen and sulphur, then during sodium fusion it generally forms sodium thiocyanate:

$Na+C+N+S \rightarrow NaSCN$

Sodium thiocyanate gives a blood-red colour with ferric ions due to formation of ferric thiocyanate complex, not Prussian blue.

Prussian blue colour is obtained in the test for nitrogen when sodium cyanide is formed:

$NaCN+FeSO_{4} \rightarrow Na_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]$

On acidification, it gives Prussian blue.

But for a compound having both N and S together, the characteristic test is blood-red colour due to thiocyanate, not Prussian blue.

So, the correct answer is:

$\text{Option D: Statement I is true but Statement II is false}$

Statement D : An organic compound is pure if the mixed melting point remains the same. This statement is correct. If mixing a small quantity of an unknown compound with a known compound does not change the melting point, this suggests the unknown compound is the same as the known and thus pure. Based on the analysis, the correct statements are A, C, and D. Option A : A, C, D only.

questions.explanation_text: The correct option for the purification of steam volatile water-immiscible substances is Option D, Steam distillation. Steam distillation is a separation technique used to purify or isolate temperature-sensitive materials, such as natural aromatic compounds, that are volatile in steam at a temperature that is lower than their decomposition temperatures. It exploits the fact that immiscible liquids can be distilled at a lower temperature than the boiling points of the individual components. Here is how steam distillation works: Water and the other immiscible substance are placed in the distillation apparatus. Steam is generated either within the same flask or introduced from an external source. The hot steam helps vaporize the other substance at a temperature below its normal boiling point. The vapors of water and the volatile substance both pass into the condenser, where they are cooled. Upon cooling, the vapors convert back into liquid, which is then collected in a separate container. Since the two substances are immiscible, they separate into two distinct layers, typically, with the organic compound floating on top of the water or sinking below it, depending on their densities. The layers can then be separated using a separating funnel or other means. Steam distillation is different from fractional distillation (Option A), which is used for the separation of a mixture into its component parts, or fractions, of compounds that are miscible and have different boiling points. Fractional distillation often involves the use of a fractionating column, which brings more efficiency in separating substances with close boiling points. Simple distillation (Option B) is suitable for separating a liquid from impurities or for separating liquids with significantly different boiling points (usually the difference in boiling points should be at least $25^{\circ}C$ ). On the other hand, fractional distillation under reduced pressure (Option C) is used when a liquid has a very high boiling point or might decompose at high temperatures. By reducing the pressure, the boiling point of the liquid is lowered and it can be distilled at a temperature much lower than its normal boiling point, thus avoiding decomposition. Therefore, for volatile substances that are not miscible with water, steam distillation remains the ideal choice.

questions.question_text: In Kjeldahl's method for estimation of nitrogen, $CuSO_{4}$ acts as :
questions.question_html: In Kjeldahl's method for estimation of nitrogen, $CuSO_{4}$ acts as :
questions.explanation_text: The correct option here is : Option A : catalytic agent In the Kjeldahl method for the estimation of nitrogen, $CuSO_{4}$ or copper sulfate acts as a catalytic agent. The method consists of three main steps: digestion, neutralization, and titration. During the digestion phase, the organic substance containing nitrogen is heated with concentrated sulfuric acid ( $H_{2}SO_{4}$ ), which digests or breaks down the organic matrix, releasing the nitrogen in the form of ammonium sulfate ( $(NH_{4})_{2}SO_{4}$ ). Organic compound $+H_{2}SO_{4}\overset{CuSO_{4}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}(NH_{4})_{2}SO_{4}$ Catalysts such as $CuSO_{4}$ , along with other salts like potassium sulfate ( $K_{2}SO_{4}$ ), are added to the reaction mixture to raise the boiling point of the sulfuric acid and to accelerate the oxidation of the organic material. This increases the rate of the digestion process, ensuring that the nitrogen within the sample is fully converted to ammonium ions ( $NH_{4}^{+}$ ). The catalyst itself is not consumed in the reaction and does not become a part of the product; its role is to increase the reaction rate. After digestion, the mixture is neutralized with a base, and then the liberated ammonia is distilled off and quantitatively measured, typically by titration with a standard acid solution. Therefore, $CuSO_{4}$ serves as a catalyst in this chemical analysis technique for quantitatively determining the nitrogen content of organic substances.

questions.question_text: Following Kjeldahl's method, $1g$ of organic compound released ammonia, that neutralised $10mL$ of $2MH_{2}SO_{4}$ . The percentage of nitrogen in the compound is ___________ $%$ .
questions.question_html: Following Kjeldahl's method, $1g$ of organic compound released ammonia, that neutralised $10mL$ of $2MH_{2}SO_{4}$ . The percentage of nitrogen in the compound is ___________ $%$ .
questions.explanation_text: To determine the percentage of nitrogen using the Kjeldahl's method, we first need to find out how much ammonia (NH 3 ) was produced and then calculate the equivalent amount of nitrogen in the sample. The ammonia released reacts with sulfuric acid (H 2 SO 4 ) in the following stoichiometry : $2NH_{3}+H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow (NH_{4})_{2}SO_{4}$ Each mole of H 2 SO 4 reacts with 2 moles of NH 3 . Since 10 mL of 2 M sulfuric acid is neutralized by the ammonia, we can calculate the amount (in moles) of ammonia : $n(NH_{3})=2 \times n(H_{2}SO_{4})$ Now calculate the moles of H 2 SO 4 used : $n(H_{2}SO_{4})=M \times V$ $n(H_{2}SO_{4})=2M \times 10mL \times \frac{1L}{1000mL}$ $n(H_{2}SO_{4})=0.02mol$ Therefore, the number of moles of NH 3 released will be twice that of the moles of H 2 SO 4 neutralized : $n(NH_{3})=2 \times 0.02mol$ $n(NH_{3})=0.04mol$ Next, we use the molar mass of nitrogen (14 g/mol) to find the mass of nitrogen : $m(N)=n(N) \times M(N)$ $m(N)=0.04mol \times 14g/mol$ $m(N)=0.56g$ To find the percentage of nitrogen in the compound, we take the mass of nitrogen divided by the mass of the original sample and multiply by 100% : $Percentnitrogen=(\frac{m(N)}{m(sample)}) \times 100%$ $Percentnitrogen=(\frac{0.56g}{1g}) \times 100%$ $Percentnitrogen=56%$ The percentage of nitrogen in the compound is 56%.
questions.explanation_html:

The ammonia released reacts with sulfuric acid (H2SO4) in the following stoichiometry :

$2NH_{3}+H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow (NH_{4})_{2}SO_{4}$

Each mole of H2SO4 reacts with 2 moles of NH3. Since 10 mL of 2 M sulfuric acid is neutralized by the ammonia, we can calculate the amount (in moles) of ammonia :

$n(NH_{3})=2 \times n(H_{2}SO_{4})$

Now calculate the moles of H2SO4 used :

$n(H_{2}SO_{4})=M \times V$

$n(H_{2}SO_{4})=2M \times 10mL \times \frac{1L}{1000mL}$

$n(H_{2}SO_{4})=0.02mol$

Therefore, the number of moles of NH3 released will be twice that of the moles of H2SO4 neutralized :

$n(NH_{3})=2 \times 0.02mol$

$n(NH_{3})=0.04mol$

Next, we use the molar mass of nitrogen (14 g/mol) to find the mass of nitrogen :

$m(N)=n(N) \times M(N)$

$m(N)=0.04mol \times 14g/mol$

$m(N)=0.56g$

To find the percentage of nitrogen in the compound, we take the mass of nitrogen divided by the mass of the original sample and multiply by 100% :

$Percentnitrogen=(\frac{m(N)}{m(sample)}) \times 100%$

$Percentnitrogen=(\frac{0.56g}{1g}) \times 100%$

$Percentnitrogen=56%$

The percentage of nitrogen in the compound is 56%.

Methyl orange exists in two resonance forms: a benzenoid form (yellow) and a quinonoid form (red). In acidic solution, the equilibrium shifts towards the quinonoid form, which is red and more intensely colored than the yellow benzenoid form. The equilibrium can be represented as follows: Yellow Benzenoid form $⇋$ Red Quinonoid form In conclusion, both statements are incorrect. questions.explanation_text: Nitrogen Detection (Lassaigne's Test) Nitrogen in organic compounds is detected by converting it into sodium cyanide, which further reacts with iron(II) sulfate to form sodium hexacyanoferrate(II). By reacting this with iron(III) ions, Prussian blue is formed: $\begin{aligned} & Na+C+N \rightarrow NaCN \\ \\ & 6NaCN+FeSO_{4} \rightarrow Na_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]+Na_{2}SO_{4} \\ \\ & Na_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]+Fe^{3+} \rightarrow Fe_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]_{3}\text{(Prussian blue)} \end{aligned}$ Sulphur Detection Sulphur can be detected using Sodium nitroprusside: $Na_{2}[Fe(CN)_{5}NO]+Na_{2}S \rightarrow Na_{4}[Fe(CN)_{5}NOS]\text{[Purple]}$ Phosphorous Detection Phosphorus detection involves reaction with ammonium molybdate to form a canary yellow compound: $\begin{aligned} & Na_{3}PO_{4}+3HNO_{3} \rightarrow H_{3}PO_{4}+3NaNO_{3} \\ \\ & H_{3}PO_{4}+12(NH_{4})_{2}MoO_{4}+21HNO_{3} \rightarrow \\ \\ & (NH_{4})_{3}PO_{4} \cdot 12MoO_{3}+21NH_{4}NO_{3}+12H_{2}O\text{(canary yellow)} \end{aligned}$ Halogen Detection Halogens react with silver nitrate to form specific colored precipitates: $\begin{aligned} & NaCl+AgNO_{3}(aq) \rightarrow AgCl+NaNO_{3}\text{(White)} \\ \\ & NaBr+AgNO_{3}(aq) \rightarrow AgBr+NaNO_{3}\text{(Pale yellow)} \\ \\ & NaI+AgNO_{3}(aq) \rightarrow AgI+NaNO_{3}\text{(Yellow)} \end{aligned}$ Based on the above reactions, the correct matching is: Option A A-III (Nitrogen), B-I (Sulphur), C-IV (Phosphorous), D-II (Halogen).
questions.explanation_html:
Nitrogen Detection (Lassaigne's Test)

Nitrogen in organic compounds is detected by converting it into sodium cyanide, which further reacts with iron(II) sulfate to form sodium hexacyanoferrate(II). By reacting this with iron(III) ions, Prussian blue is formed:

$\begin{aligned} & Na+C+N \rightarrow NaCN \\ \\ & 6NaCN+FeSO_{4} \rightarrow Na_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]+Na_{2}SO_{4} \\ \\ & Na_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]+Fe^{3+} \rightarrow Fe_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]_{3}\text{(Prussian blue)} \end{aligned}$

Sulphur Detection

Sulphur can be detected using Sodium nitroprusside:

$Na_{2}[Fe(CN)_{5}NO]+Na_{2}S \rightarrow Na_{4}[Fe(CN)_{5}NOS]\text{[Purple]}$

Phosphorous Detection

Phosphorus detection involves reaction with ammonium molybdate to form a canary yellow compound:

$\begin{aligned} & Na_{3}PO_{4}+3HNO_{3} \rightarrow H_{3}PO_{4}+3NaNO_{3} \\ \\ & H_{3}PO_{4}+12(NH_{4})_{2}MoO_{4}+21HNO_{3} \rightarrow \\ \\ & (NH_{4})_{3}PO_{4} \cdot 12MoO_{3}+21NH_{4}NO_{3}+12H_{2}O\text{(canary yellow)} \end{aligned}$

Halogen Detection

Halogens react with silver nitrate to form specific colored precipitates:

$\begin{aligned} & NaCl+AgNO_{3}(aq) \rightarrow AgCl+NaNO_{3}\text{(White)} \\ \\ & NaBr+AgNO_{3}(aq) \rightarrow AgBr+NaNO_{3}\text{(Pale yellow)} \\ \\ & NaI+AgNO_{3}(aq) \rightarrow AgI+NaNO_{3}\text{(Yellow)} \end{aligned}$

Based on the above reactions, the correct matching is:

Option A

A-III (Nitrogen), B-I (Sulphur), C-IV (Phosphorous), D-II (Halogen).

questions.question_html:

[Atomic masses (in u) Mn = 55; Cl = 35.5; O = 16, I = 127, Na = 23, K = 39, S = 32]
questions.explanation_text: First Step : MnO 2 + 4HCl $\rightarrow$ MnCl 2 + Cl 2 + 2H 2 O Here 1 mol of MnO 2 produce 1 mol of Cl 2 $\therefore$ Mole ratio of $n_{MnO_{2}}:n_{Cl_{2}}=1:1$ Second Step : Cl 2 + 2KI $\rightarrow$ 2KCl + I 2 Here, 1 mol of Cl 2 produce 1 mol of I 2 Mole ratio of $n_{Cl_{2}}:n_{I_{2}}=1:1$ Third Step : I 2 + 2Na 2 S 2 O 3 $\rightarrow$ 2NaI + Na 2 S 2 O 3 1 mol of I 2 react with 2 mol of Na 2 S 2 O 3 Mole ratio of $n_{I_{2}}:n_{N_{2}S_{2}O_{3}}=1:2$ Given Na 2 S 2 O 3 is 60 mL of 0.1 M $\therefore$ Number of moles of Na 2 S 2 O 3 = V (in L) $\times$ M (Molarity) = $\frac{60}{1000} \times 0.1$ = 0.006 mol $\therefore$ Number of moles of I 2 $=\frac{1}{2}(0.006)$ = 0.003 $\therefore$ Moles of MnO 2 = 0.003 (as mole ratio of MnO 2 and Cl 2 = 1 : 1) Molar mass of MnO 2 = 55 + 32 = 87 $\therefore$ Mass of MnO 2 = 0.003 $\times$ 87 = 0.261 gm Given MnO 2 = 2g $\therefore$ % of MnO 2 = $\frac{0.261}{2} \times 100=13%$
questions.explanation_html:
First Step :

MnO2 + 4HCl $\rightarrow$ MnCl2 + Cl2 + 2H2O

Here 1 mol of MnO2 produce 1 mol of Cl2

$\therefore$ Mole ratio of $n_{MnO_{2}}:n_{Cl_{2}}=1:1$

Second Step :

Cl2 + 2KI $\rightarrow$ 2KCl + I2

Here, 1 mol of Cl2 produce 1 mol of I2

Mole ratio of $n_{Cl_{2}}:n_{I_{2}}=1:1$

Third Step :

I2 + 2Na2S2O3 $\rightarrow$ 2NaI + Na2S2O3

1 mol of I2 react with 2 mol of Na2S2O3

Mole ratio of $n_{I_{2}}:n_{N_{2}S_{2}O_{3}}=1:2$

Given Na2S2O3 is 60 mL of 0.1 M

$\therefore$ Number of moles of Na2S2O3

= V (in L) $\times$ M (Molarity)

= $\frac{60}{1000} \times 0.1$

= 0.006 mol

$\therefore$ Number of moles of I2

$=\frac{1}{2}(0.006)$

= 0.003

$\therefore$ Moles of MnO2 = 0.003 (as mole ratio of MnO2 and Cl2 = 1 : 1)

Molar mass of MnO2 = 55 + 32 = 87

$\therefore$ Mass of MnO2 = 0.003 $\times$ 87 = 0.261 gm

Given MnO2 = 2g

$\therefore$ % of MnO2 = $\frac{0.261}{2} \times 100=13%$

questions.question_html: Acidic ferric chloride solution on treatment with excess of potassium ferrocyanide gives a Prussian blue coloured colloidal species. It is :
questions.explanation_text: Prussian blue is a complex compound that has the formula $\text{Fe}_{4}[\text{Fe(CN)}_{6}]_{3}$ . It is formed by the reaction of ferric ions with ferrocyanide ions. The reaction can be explained as follows: Potassium ferrocyanide, $\text{K}_{4}[\text{Fe(CN)}_{6}]$ , dissociates in water to release ferrocyanide ions, $[\text{Fe(CN)}_{6}]^{4-}$ . The ferric ions, $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ , present in the acidic ferric chloride solution will react with the ferrocyanide ions. In an acidic medium, the ferric ions hydrolyze, forming a complex with ferrocyanide ions, leading to the formation of Prussian blue. The overall reaction can be represented as: $\text{Fe}^{3+}+4[\text{Fe(CN)}_{6}]^{4-} \rightarrow \text{Fe}_{4}[\text{Fe(CN)}_{6}]_{3}$ The Prussian blue complex is a colloidal species and exhibits an intense blue color. It has been historically used as a pigment in paints and also has applications in medical treatments as an antidote for certain types of heavy metal poisoning.
questions.explanation_html:
Prussian blue is a complex compound that has the formula $\text{Fe}_{4}[\text{Fe(CN)}_{6}]_{3}$ . It is formed by the reaction of ferric ions with ferrocyanide ions.

The reaction can be explained as follows:

  1. Potassium ferrocyanide, $\text{K}_{4}[\text{Fe(CN)}_{6}]$ , dissociates in water to release ferrocyanide ions, $[\text{Fe(CN)}_{6}]^{4-}$ .


  2. The ferric ions, $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ , present in the acidic ferric chloride solution will react with the ferrocyanide ions.


  3. In an acidic medium, the ferric ions hydrolyze, forming a complex with ferrocyanide ions, leading to the formation of Prussian blue.

The overall reaction can be represented as:

$\text{Fe}^{3+}+4[\text{Fe(CN)}_{6}]^{4-} \rightarrow \text{Fe}_{4}[\text{Fe(CN)}_{6}]_{3}$

The Prussian blue complex is a colloidal species and exhibits an intense blue color. It has been historically used as a pigment in paints and also has applications in medical treatments as an antidote for certain types of heavy metal poisoning.
